description: The average number of orders per account counts all accounts, with zero for accounts that have no orders.

c.request: For each account with standing orders (`order.account_id`), count its orders. Which accounts have more orders than the average number of orders per account? For each, show the account id, its order count, how far the count is above that average, and how far the count is above the average order count of those above-average accounts. Sort by this last difference from largest to smallest and give only the first 10. Don't round anything. The average number of orders per account counts all accounts, with zero for accounts that have no orders.
c.sql: WITH order_counts AS (SELECT a.account_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM account AS a LEFT JOIN `order` AS o ON o.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.account_id), overall AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_order_count FROM order_counts), above_average AS (SELECT oc.account_id, oc.order_count FROM order_counts AS oc CROSS JOIN overall AS ov WHERE oc.order_count > ov.avg_order_count), above_average_mean AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_above_average_count FROM above_average) SELECT aa.account_id, aa.order_count, aa.order_count - ov.avg_order_count AS above_overall_average, aa.order_count - am.avg_above_average_count AS above_above_average_mean FROM above_average AS aa CROSS JOIN overall AS ov CROSS JOIN above_average_mean AS am ORDER BY above_above_average_mean DESC, aa.account_id LIMIT 10;

b.request: Count standing orders for each account, including zero for accounts with no orders; select accounts whose count exceeds the average count across all accounts, and show each account ID, its count, its difference from that overall average, and its difference from the average count among the selected accounts. Sort by the last difference descending and return the first 10 without rounding
b.sql: WITH order_counts AS (SELECT a.account_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM account AS a LEFT JOIN `order` AS o ON o.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.account_id), overall AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_count FROM order_counts), selected AS (SELECT oc.account_id, oc.order_count, ov.avg_count AS overall_avg FROM order_counts AS oc CROSS JOIN overall AS ov WHERE oc.order_count > ov.avg_count), selected_avg AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_count FROM selected) SELECT s.account_id, s.order_count, s.order_count - s.overall_avg AS difference_from_overall_average, s.order_count - sa.avg_count AS difference_from_selected_average FROM selected AS s CROSS JOIN selected_avg AS sa ORDER BY difference_from_selected_average DESC, s.account_id LIMIT 10

a.request: For each account with standing orders (`order.account_id`), count its orders. Work out the average number of orders per account, averaging over every account in `account`, with accounts that have no orders counting as zero. Keep the accounts whose order count is above that average. For each, show the account id, its order count, how far the count is above that average, and how far the count is above the average order count of the kept above-average accounts. Sort by this last difference from largest to smallest and return only the first 10 rows. Don't round anything.
a.sql: WITH order_counts AS (SELECT a.account_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM account AS a LEFT JOIN `order` AS o ON o.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.account_id), overall_average AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_orders FROM order_counts), kept AS (SELECT oc.account_id, oc.order_count, oa.avg_orders FROM order_counts AS oc CROSS JOIN overall_average AS oa WHERE oc.order_count > oa.avg_orders), kept_average AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS avg_kept_orders FROM kept) SELECT k.account_id, k.order_count, k.order_count - k.avg_orders AS above_overall_average, k.order_count - ka.avg_kept_orders AS above_kept_average FROM kept AS k CROSS JOIN kept_average AS ka ORDER BY above_kept_average DESC, k.account_id LIMIT 10;

d.request: For each account, count its standing orders using `order.account_id`, treating accounts with no orders as having zero. Calculate the average order count across all accounts, including those with zero orders. Which accounts have more orders than that average? For each, show the account ID, its order count, the amount above the overall average, and the amount above the average order count among above-average accounts. Sort by the last difference in descending order and return only the first 10. Do not round any values.
d.sql: WITH order_counts AS (SELECT a.account_id, COUNT(o.order_id) AS order_count FROM account AS a LEFT JOIN `order` AS o ON o.account_id = a.account_id GROUP BY a.account_id), overall AS (SELECT AVG(order_count) AS average_order_count FROM order_counts), above_average AS (SELECT oc.account_id, oc.order_count, oc.order_count - overall.average_order_count AS above_overall_average FROM order_counts AS oc CROSS JOIN overall WHERE oc.order_count > overall.average_order_count) SELECT account_id, order_count, above_overall_average, order_count - (SELECT AVG(order_count) FROM above_average) AS above_above_average FROM above_average ORDER BY above_above_average DESC, account_id LIMIT 10;
